paragraphs: The vestibulo-ocular reflex moves the eyes to keep images stable while the head moves. For a distant target, the eyes typically rotate at roughly the same speed as the head in the opposite direction. The paper addresses why this simple relationship must change with eye position, the angle between the eyes, and head translation.

The authors first construct a model of the required motion using sensory signals available to the nervous system. These include head rotation from the semicircular canals, head translation from the otoliths, and signals representing eye position and vergence. They then develop a dynamical model that describes how the response unfolds over time.

Compared with monkey eye movements, the dynamical model reproduces both the size and timing of contextual changes in the reflex. It suggests a possible way for the cerebellum and brain stem to combine the necessary signals. It also predicts how neurons in the eye movement system should respond when several inputs act together.
neurips-1995-a-dynamical-model-of-contex.tldr: A dynamical model explains how head motion and eye configuration jointly adjust the reflex that stabilizes vision.

paragraphs: This paper treats robot navigation as a problem of building an internal state that makes the right action unambiguous. The robot receives local sensory information, while its task concerns movement through an environment. The proposed solution is to represent desired paths within an internal space constructed from the robot's sensory experience.

A recurrent neural network builds this representation from sensory inputs arriving over time. Its internal state therefore reflects the temporal sensory sequence, providing the basis for a unique mapping from state to motor command. The central idea is that learning useful navigation behavior also involves learning an adequate representation of the situation.

Experiments use a real robot equipped with a laser range sensor. The authors report robust navigation through coordination between the robot's internal dynamics and its environment. They also report that this coordination becomes structurally stable as the coupled system organizes a global attractor. The result connects reliable navigation to the behavior of the robot and environment as a combined dynamical system.
neurips-1995-a-dynamical-systems-approac.tldr: A recurrent network learns internal dynamics that support robust navigation from a robot's local sensory history.

paragraphs: Recognizing an object from feature points requires deciding which points correspond even when the object changes shape. This paper develops a matching framework that starts with an affine transformation, then adds multiple feature types and spatial regions that can undergo local transformations. These additions allow the representation to accommodate non-rigid changes.

The algorithm alternates between updating the transformation and updating the point correspondences. The affine transformation has a closed-form solution, allowing that component to work with data of any dimension. Correspondences are handled by softassign, a method that enforces assignment constraints in both directions between the point sets.

The approach matters because it combines richer object descriptions with a manageable matching procedure. The authors state that adding non-rigid transformations and multiple features preserves the computational complexity of the underlying affine point-matching algorithm. They provide results on synthetic and real data, including two- and three-dimensional point sets and two-dimensional objects described by several feature types and parts.
neurips-1995-a-framework-for-non-rigid-m.tldr: An alternating matching framework combines soft assignments, multiple features, and local transformations to handle non-rigid objects.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a mechanism that lets a neural network both organize sensory representations and recall learned associations. Its key idea is to suppress transmission through feedback connections during learning. The biological motivation is experimental evidence of cholinergic suppression at feedback synapses in cortical layer I, without corresponding suppression at feedforward synapses in layer IV.

During learning, the network receives both the sensory stimulus and the desired response as inputs. Feedforward connections organize representations of the stimuli, while feedback connections learn connectivity corresponding to the transpose of the feedforward connections. Suppressing feedback transmission changes how those connections influence ongoing activity while the associations are being learned.

During recall, the suppression is lifted. A sensory input activates its organized representation, and network activity produces the learned response. Using local learning rules, the network learns mappings that are not linearly separable. The contribution is a concrete proposal for coordinating representation learning and associative recall through different transmission conditions during learning and retrieval.
neurips-1995-cholinergic-suppression-of-.tldr: Suppressing feedback transmission during learning may let cortical networks combine self-organized representations with associative recall.

paragraphs: A hierarchical mixture of experts arranges specialized predictors in a tree. This paper asks how that tree can change during training instead of retaining a fixed structure. It introduces two complementary operations: growing the tree when additional experts are warranted and pruning branches to reduce unnecessary computation or redundant structure.

Growth uses a likelihood-based splitting criterion applied to each expert. This makes expansion depend on the learning process. The pruning procedure considers only the most probable path through the tree, allowing other branches to be omitted temporarily or removed permanently when they become redundant. The two operations address where capacity is added and where computation is spent.

The authors demonstrate the algorithms on classification involving two interlocking spirals and eight-bit parity patterns. They report substantial speed improvements and more efficient parameter use relative to the standard fixed tree. These findings support adapting the organization of the experts alongside their learned parameters, rather than treating the architecture as settled before training begins.
neurips-1995-constructive-algorithms-for.tldr: Growing and pruning a hierarchy of experts during training improves speed and parameter efficiency on the reported classification tasks.

paragraphs: Neurons can show related activity at different time scales. Their spikes may occur close together in time, and their total spike counts over an entire trial may also vary together. This paper examines the connection between these two observations using pairs of simultaneously recorded neurons from a previous study of macaque visual area MT.

The analysis relates correlations in trial-level spike counts to peaks in cross-correlograms, which describe the timing relationship between two spike trains. The peaks have widths on the order of ten milliseconds, whereas the spike counts cover two-second trials. The question is whether a shared source can account for correlations observed across these very different windows.

The authors conclude that common input responsible for the short-time peaks also produces the correlations in whole-trial spike counts. They argue that shared excitation and shared inhibition can both contribute. The result connects fine temporal coordination with slower count variability, giving the two measurements a common mechanistic interpretation in these recordings.
neurips-1995-correlated-neuronal-respons.tldr: Shared input links millisecond-scale spike coordination to correlations in neuronal spike counts over two-second trials.

paragraphs: This paper studies how Bayesian networks can represent relationships among continuous variables. Such a network organizes a probability model around dependencies between variables. The authors use nonlinear conditional density estimators, which describe how the probability distribution of one variable changes with the values of other variables connected to it.

The work addresses both discovering structure and using the resulting model. For structure discovery, the authors demonstrate that useful relationships can emerge from a dataset through self-organization. The emphasis is on extracting an organization from the observations, so the network provides a description of how continuous quantities depend on one another.

For inference, the paper presents sampling methods for updating beliefs using conditional density models based on Markov blankets. A Markov blanket identifies the local variables needed to determine a variable's conditional distribution within the network. This gives the sampling procedure a local basis while serving the broader task of updating beliefs. Together, the contributions connect learned dependency structure with probabilistic reasoning over continuous data.
neurips-1995-discovering-structure-in-co.tldr: Nonlinear conditional density models support self-organized Bayesian network structure and sampling-based belief updates for continuous variables.

paragraphs: Goal-directed attention needs to persist long enough to support an activity while remaining able to shift quickly when circumstances change. This paper frames those requirements as a dynamical problem. The authors argue that long maintenance and rapid transition impose conflicting demands within linear dynamics, motivating a nonlinear mechanism.

Their proposed mechanism is a sigmoid unit that feeds its output back into itself and operates near a saddle-node bifurcation. A bifurcation marks a qualitative change in a system's dynamics. Operating near this transition provides a candidate way for the same unit to support both sustained attention and quick switching.

The authors also examine recurrent networks in simulated bug-eat-food tasks set in changing environments. They show that behavior near a saddle-node bifurcation can emerge as a functional property supporting survival. This links the proposed mechanism to the demands of acting in an environment: the relevant dynamics arise in networks facing a need to maintain useful behavior while responding to change.
neurips-1995-dynamics-of-attention-as-ne.tldr: Dynamics near a saddle-node bifurcation offer a mechanism for attention that both persists and switches rapidly.

paragraphs: Allocating capacity in a telecommunications network requires decisions quickly enough to meet operational response constraints. This paper investigates neural controllers that approximate the allocations produced by a linear programming optimizer. The motivation is to retain much of the optimizer's traffic throughput while reducing the time needed to produce a decision.

The authors evaluate two combinations: a feedforward network with a heuristic, and a feedforward network with a recurrent network. The linear programming optimizer serves two roles. It supplies labeled examples for training the feedforward network, and it provides the benchmark against which the completed controllers are evaluated.

The feedforward-plus-heuristic system achieves 99% of the optimizer's throughput, while the feedforward-plus-recurrent system achieves 95%. Once trained, both neural approaches produce solutions in a fraction of the optimizer's time. The results make the tradeoff concrete: learning from optimization outputs can yield faster capacity decisions while preserving a high proportion of the throughput obtained by the original optimization procedure.
neurips-1995-experiments-with-neural-net.tldr: Neural capacity controllers achieve 99% and 95% of linear programming throughput while producing decisions much faster after training.

paragraphs: Sigmoid belief networks represent probabilistic relationships compactly, but learning their parameters can require expensive calculations over hidden variables. The paper identifies exact expectation-maximization as intractable even when the network has relatively few hidden units. This creates a practical obstacle to using the models for supervised and unsupervised learning.

The authors replace exact likelihood calculations with bounds on those likelihoods. They introduce extended and complementary representations of the networks, then perform parameter estimation in these alternative forms. In either representation, the estimation problem can be reduced to quadratic optimization, providing a tractable route around the expensive expectation step.

The significance is that changing the representation and objective calculation makes learning more manageable while retaining a probabilistic modeling framework. The method directly targets the computation that prevents exact parameter estimation from being practical. The authors also state that complementary networks can estimate continuous probability densities, extending the role of that representation beyond its use in accelerating learning.
neurips-1995-fast-learning-by-bounding-l.tldr: Likelihood bounds and alternative network representations reduce difficult sigmoid belief-network parameter estimation to quadratic optimization.

paragraphs: This paper examines the computational capabilities of Recurrent Cascade-Correlation, or RCC, by comparing it with finite-state automata. A finite-state automaton processes inputs through transitions among a finite collection of states. It therefore supplies a precise reference for asking which state-dependent computations a recurrent neural architecture can represent.

The authors present a theoretical analysis establishing that a large class of finite-state automata cannot be realized by RCC. The contribution is a proof about the architecture's representational capacity. It identifies computations that fall outside what the model can express, rather than reporting difficulty encountered by a particular training run.

The finding matters because some recurrent networks are equivalent in computational power to finite-state automata, but that property does not carry over to RCC. Having recurrent connections alone does not establish the same representational capabilities across architectures. The paper therefore supplies a structural limit that must be considered when choosing RCC for tasks requiring particular finite-state behavior.
neurips-1995-finite-state-automata-that-.tldr: A theoretical proof shows that Recurrent Cascade-Correlation cannot represent a large class of finite-state automata.

paragraphs: This paper introduces an incremental regression system made of locally linear experts. Each expert learns independently, without competing with the others for training data. Cooperation happens when a prediction is requested: the system blends the experts' individual outputs. This separates the process of learning local models from the process of combining their answers.

Each expert minimizes a penalized local cross-validation error using second-order optimization. It adjusts the size and shape of the region where its predictions apply, effectively learning its own local distance measure. It also adjusts the importance assigned to individual input dimensions, allowing it to detect features relevant to its prediction task.

The authors derive asymptotic results and use simulations to examine interference, learning speed, accuracy, feature detection, and task-oriented incremental learning. The approach matters because each local predictor can adapt both its fitted relationship and its definition of locality. Blending then brings these separately developed views together when the system needs to answer a specific query.
neurips-1995-from-isolation-to-cooperati.tldr: Independent local experts learn their own relevant features and regions, then cooperate by blending predictions.

paragraphs: This paper presents an offline handwritten word recognizer that combines radial basis function networks with hidden Markov models. The two components have distinct roles. The neural networks estimate emission probabilities associated with the Markov states, supplying probabilities that connect image evidence to the states used by the sequence model.

The proposed extension makes these estimates contextual. When processing the current image segment, the network also uses left context represented by the preceding segment in the sequence. The probability assigned to the current visual evidence can therefore depend on what came immediately before it. This changes the information used at the emission-estimation stage of recognition.

The reported result is that the contextual system does not outperform the earlier system without context, although it behaves differently. That distinction is central to interpreting the contribution: including neighboring information changes the recognizer, but the comparison does not establish an improvement in overall performance. The paper explores a specific way to incorporate context within a hybrid neural and probabilistic sequence architecture.
neurips-1995-handwritten-word-recognitio.tldr: Adding preceding-segment context changes a hybrid handwriting recognizer's behavior but does not improve on its context-free predecessor.

paragraphs: Learning from sequences requires preserving information that may become useful much later. The paper starts from the difficulty of extracting these long-term dependencies in recurrent networks and hidden Markov models. It notes that researchers have addressed the problem by giving hidden states meanings based on knowledge of a particular application.

The authors propose a more general structural assumption: temporal dependencies form a hierarchy. Under this assumption, information needed over long intervals should be represented by variables that evolve over long time scales. They apply the principle to a recurrent network with delays and multiple time scales, giving different parts of the model different temporal roles.

Experiments confirm advantages for these structures. The authors also propose extending the same organizing principle to hidden Markov models and input/output hidden Markov models. The contribution is a way to use prior knowledge about the organization of time without specifying the meaning of every hidden variable. Its usefulness rests on representing long-lived context through correspondingly slow internal variables.
neurips-1995-hierarchical-recurrent-neur.tldr: Hierarchical recurrent networks use delays and multiple time scales to make long-term sequence dependencies easier to represent.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning as an ongoing sequence of tasks. A learner that has already solved earlier tasks has accumulated knowledge that might help with later ones. The central question is whether that experience allows it to learn a new task from fewer examples while making more accurate predictions on unseen cases.

The authors describe several approaches to lifelong learning and apply them to object recognition. Their common purpose is to transfer knowledge between tasks. The relevant unit of experience is therefore the stream of tasks: learning on one part of that stream can influence how effectively the learner handles another part.

Across the approaches examined, the paper reports consistently better generalization with less training data, attributed to knowledge transfer. The finding supports treating previous learning as a resource for future learning. In the reported object-recognition setting, experience across tasks improves the relationship between how much new data is needed and how accurately the resulting model generalizes.
neurips-1995-is-learning-the-n-th-thing-.tldr: Across the tested object-recognition approaches, transferring knowledge between tasks improves generalization while reducing training-data needs.

paragraphs: The paper addresses optimization when measurements are noisy and every experiment is expensive. In this setting, an optimizer must make productive use of the observations it has already collected. The proposed algorithms build a global nonlinear model of expected output while also performing Bayesian analysis of locally weighted polynomial models.

The local models provide estimates of uncertainty, noise, gradients, and curvature. These quantities guide automated decisions resembling those a practitioner would make in response surface methodology. Global and local information are brought together through locally weighted regression, linking the broader response model with detailed information around a candidate operating region.

The authors investigate whether the global model helps optimization and extend the approach to functions that change over time. Comparisons use randomly generated functions and a simulated manufacturing task against a carefully tuned higher-order stochastic optimizer. They report improvements in total regret, convergence time, and final solution quality. The findings support using accumulated observations for both modeling the response and directing subsequent expensive experiments.
neurips-1995-memory-based-stochastic-opt.tldr: Combining global response models with local Bayesian estimates improves optimization when experiments are noisy and costly.

paragraphs: This paper presents neural-network-based control for two kinds of nonlinear dynamical systems. The common challenge is selecting control actions when the relationship between the system and its controller is difficult to establish. The work centers on whether the proposed controllers can make the resulting feedback system stable.

The first kind of system has uncertain parameters that enter its dynamics nonlinearly. The uncertainty therefore concerns quantities whose influence is itself nonlinear. The second kind consists of systems for which a stabilizing control structure cannot be determined. These are distinct obstacles: uncertainty about nonlinear parameter effects and difficulty identifying a suitable form of stabilizing control.

The authors show that their neural controllers produce closed-loop stability under certain conditions. Closed-loop stability concerns the system operating together with its feedback controller, so the result addresses the behavior of the combined arrangement. The qualification matters: the claim is conditional, rather than a guarantee for every nonlinear system. The contribution establishes a stability-oriented basis for neural control across the two stated problem classes.
neurips-1995-neural-control-for-nonlinea.tldr: Neural controllers provide conditional closed-loop stability for two challenging classes of nonlinear systems.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether shared features of neural codes can follow from a common optimization principle. It studies a model that linearly filters an input and generates spikes through threshold crossings. When the threshold is chosen to maximize transmitted information, the model naturally produces features seen across a range of creatures.

This optimization requires adaptation to more than the average signal level. The neuron must also adapt to the statistical structure of both signals and noise. The result gives apparently separate coding observations a shared explanation: they can arise from adjusting a threshold to preserve information under the prevailing input conditions.

The authors also introduce a method for calculating mutual information between a spike train and a selected aspect of its input without reconstructing the input signal. The formulation assumes small correlations within the spike train, and they provide a procedure for checking that assumption. This analytical contribution complements the model by offering a way to quantify information while explicitly testing a condition required by the calculation.
neurips-1995-optimization-principles-for.tldr: Maximizing transmitted information in a threshold-crossing neuron model explains shared coding features and requires adaptation to signal and noise statistics.

paragraphs: Topographic brain mappings organize features across a neural surface. A common modeling approach places those features in a low-dimensional geometric space and uses a self-organizing algorithm to map them onto two dimensions. This paper questions two choices embedded in that approach: how similarity is represented and how the mapping's objective is defined.

The authors propose allowing similarities that need not be geometric distances. They also advocate explicitly choosing the objective for topographic matching, making clear what the mapping is intended to optimize. This separates the desired organization from the particular self-organizing procedure used to generate it.

They analyze an example involving interdigitated mappings, where different representations form interleaving spatial patterns. Ocular dominance columns in primary visual cortex provide the motivating example. The contribution is a more general way to formulate and study cortical organization: specify the relevant feature similarities and the matching objective directly, then examine the resulting structure. This makes the assumptions governing a map available for explicit mathematical analysis.
neurips-1995-optimizing-cortical-mapping.tldr: Explicit objectives and non-geometric feature similarities provide a more general framework for analyzing cortical maps.

paragraphs: This paper describes two parallel analog chip architectures that combine measurements of visual motion. Their inputs come from arrays of elementary velocity sensors, which together provide optical flow data. The architectures use that distributed information to estimate heading direction and time-to-contact, two quantities relevant to movement through an environment.

For heading direction, the authors use simulations to study the most important qualitative properties of the optical flow field. Those simulations help them select the functional operators used in the architecture. The design process therefore connects the structure of the visual motion signal to the computations implemented by the hardware.

For time-to-contact, the architecture uses the divergence theorem to combine information from all of its velocity sensors. Pooling those measurements is intended to average out possible errors. The two designs illustrate complementary uses of distributed sensing: selecting operations suited to the overall flow pattern and integrating many local measurements into a shared estimate. Parallel analog circuitry provides the common implementation framework.
neurips-1995-parallel-analog-vlsi-archit.tldr: Two parallel analog architectures integrate optical flow measurements to estimate heading direction and time-to-contact.

paragraphs: This paper studies how much data is needed to fit recurrent perceptron classifiers. These models extend the classical perceptron by accounting for relationships among input coordinates produced by linear digital filtering. The learning problem therefore includes structured dependencies within the input representation, and the analysis addresses the corresponding requirements on training data.

The main contribution is a set of tight sample-complexity bounds for fitting these models to experimental observations. Sample complexity describes the amount of data associated with learning a model. Providing tight bounds aims to characterize that requirement closely, rather than supplying only a loose statement that learning is possible with sufficiently many examples.

The result connects a particular extension of the perceptron to a quantitative theory of learning from data. Its relevance comes from analyzing the classifier together with the filtering-induced dependencies it is designed to handle. The paper's stated finding is about data requirements: it characterizes the sample complexity of fitting this model class, rather than reporting an empirical comparison of prediction accuracy.
neurips-1995-sample-complexity-for-learn.tldr: The paper derives tight sample-complexity bounds for recurrent perceptrons that account for dependencies induced by linear digital filtering.

paragraphs: Many combinatorial optimization problems require assignments that satisfy constraints in two directions. This paper applies softassign to the traveling salesman problem and graph partitioning. Softassign comes from recurrent neural network and statistical physics approaches, and it enforces assignment constraints without adding penalty terms to the energy being optimized.

The comparison is with softmax combined with a penalty term, an established way of handling two-way constraints in this framework. The authors also generalize softassign beyond two-way winner-take-all assignments to allow multiple membership, as required for graph partitioning. This extends the constraint-handling method to a different kind of assignment structure.

The benchmarks provide evidence of advantages in accuracy, speed, parallel execution, and algorithmic simplicity. The stated scope is optimization problems with two-way constraints. The approach matters because satisfying constraints is part of the assignment procedure itself, avoiding a separate penalty contribution to the energy function. The results indicate that this design choice can improve several practical aspects of solving the tested problems.
neurips-1995-softassign-versus-softmax-b.tldr: Softassign outperforms softmax with penalties in reported benchmarks by enforcing two-way assignment constraints directly.

paragraphs: Locating a sound requires comparing signals arriving through the two ears with very high temporal precision. This paper models spike processing in the barn owl auditory pathway, focusing on coincidence detection. The central question is how a neural system can distinguish extremely fine timing relationships despite the slower time scales of its component neurons.

The authors use an integrate-and-fire model and show that it can achieve microsecond-scale precision even when neuronal time constants are at least an order of magnitude longer. The result separates the precision of the system's timing computation from the characteristic response time of an individual modeled neuron.

A key component is an unsupervised Hebbian learning rule that fine-tunes the timing properties of neuronal connections. Learning therefore helps organize the connections needed for precise spike processing. The model offers an explanation for how auditory timing can become much sharper than neuronal time constants alone might suggest, linking connection-level adaptation to the temporal accuracy required for binaural sound localization.
neurips-1995-temporal-coding-in-the-sub-.tldr: An integrate-and-fire auditory model uses Hebbian connection tuning to achieve timing precision much finer than neuronal time constants.

paragraphs: Neural circuits often need to produce a specific trajectory through their possible states. The paper considers learning such trajectories from examples and identifies difficulties with gradient descent in networks without a useful organizing structure. It proposes constructing complex trajectories by combining simple oscillators in modular and hierarchical arrangements.

The authors examine both fast and slow oscillation regimes. Across the cases considered, they establish universal approximation properties for banks of oscillators whose frequencies are bounded. This means the proposed building blocks have broad capacity to represent target trajectories even with a restriction on their available frequencies.

The supplied text also frames a simple version of the task: adjust a network so that a single visible linear unit follows a target function over a finite time interval. This makes trajectory generation a concrete approximation problem. The central result supports oscillators as expressive components for that problem. It establishes representational capability, while the paper's motivation concerns how a structured architecture might make learning complex trajectories more workable.
neurips-1995-universal-approximation-and.tldr: Modular banks of bounded-frequency oscillators have universal approximation properties for generating trajectories.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether relationships between EEG signals can reveal changes in alertness continuously and close to real time. Alertness is assessed through errors on an auditory detection task. The work extends earlier findings about EEG spectral amplitudes by examining how signals recorded at different scalp locations relate to one another.

More frequent detection errors accompany patterns of both increased and decreased spectral coherence across several frequency bands and electrode pairs. Coherence describes relationships between signals at particular frequencies. These relationships differ between people, but their spatial and frequency patterns appear stable across recording sessions within the same person.

The authors also find that alertness changes accompany changes in correlations between EEG waveforms. Feedforward neural networks can estimate alertness from these correlations and from normalized cross-spectral information. The significance is that coordination across recording sites carries useful information about behavioral performance. Because the EEG can be recorded spontaneously and unobtrusively, the approach supports continuous monitoring, with the reported individual differences central to interpreting the signal patterns.
neurips-1995-using-feedforward-neural-ne.tldr: Feedforward networks estimate alertness from EEG relationships that track detection errors and appear stable within individuals across sessions.
